ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two sufficiently long, smooth, straight metal rails are placed parallel to each other, with a separation distance of $L$. The plane formed by the two rails and the rails themselves are inclined at an angle $\theta$ with respect to the horizontal plane. The entire setup is immersed in a uniform magnetic field with magnetic induction intensity of $B$, which is oriented perpendicular to the plane of the rails and directed upwards. Two metal rods, a and b, each with mass $m$, are placed perpendicularly on the rails. Each metal rod has a resistance of $R$ between the rails. During motion, the metal rods remain perpendicular to the rails and maintain good contact. The metal rods do not slide off the rails. The resistance of the rails is negligible. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$.

1. Initially, rod $b$ is held stationary, and rod $a$ is released from rest. Determine the magnitude of the velocity $v_{0}$ when rod $a$ reaches a state of uniform motion.
2. In the scenario of sub-question 1, when rod $a$ is moving at a uniform velocity, rod $b$ is then released from rest. Determine the magnitude of the acceleration $a_{0}$ of rod $b$ immediately after its release.
3. In the scenario of sub-question 2, starting from the instant rod $b$ is released, after a time $t_{0}$, the two rods attain the same velocity $v$. Determine the magnitude of this common velocity $v$.
4. The distance $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ that rod $a$ travels relative to rod $b$ during the time interval $t_{0}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there are two sufficiently long parallel metal guide rails, and the plane in which the guide rails lie is inclined relative to the horizontal plane; the inclination angle θ is marked on both the right side and below. Two orange metal rods a and b perpendicularly span between the two guide rails, with b located at the upper/left position and a located at the lower/right position. The pink arrow B in the figure represents the magnetic field, with direction perpendicular to the plane of the guide rails upward. Take the direction down along the inclined plane as the positive direction. Then reason: When b is fixed and a is released from rest, only the motion of a changes the area of the closed loop. When a moves with velocity v_a, the induced electromotive force is ε=BLv_a. The two rods each have resistance R, and the guide rail resistance is ignored, so the total resistance of the loop is 2R, and the current I=ε/(2R)=BLv_a/(2R). The magnitude of the Ampere force on a is F=BLI=B^2L^2v_a/(2R), and its direction hinders a from sliding down along the inclined plane. When a moves at uniform speed, the resultant force in the direction along the inclined plane is zero, so mg sinθ=B^2L^2v_0/(2R), obtaining v_0=2mgR sinθ/(B^2L^2). When a is already moving uniformly with v_0 and b has just been released, the loop current is still I=BLv_0/(2R). From the equilibrium condition in the previous question, it can be known that the magnitude of the corresponding Ampere force is BLI=mg sinθ. According to Lenz's law, at this time the Ampere force on b is down along the inclined plane, in the same direction as the component of gravity along the inclined plane, so the magnitude of the instantaneous resultant force on b is mg sinθ+mg sinθ=2mg sinθ, hence a_0=2g sinθ. After releasing b, let u=v_a-v_b. Since only relative motion changes the loop area, the induced current is determined by the relative velocity. Let k=B^2L^2/(2R), then the magnetic resistance force on a is ku, with direction opposite to the relative motion represented by u; b is subjected to an Ampere force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Thus the equations of motion of the two rods in the direction along the inclined plane are m dv_a/dt=mg sinθ-ku, m dv_b/dt=mg sinθ+ku. Adding the two equations gives d[(v_a+v_b)/2]/dt=g sinθ. At the instant of release, v_a(0)=v_0, v_b(0)=0, so the initial value of the center-of-mass velocity is v_0/2. When after t_0 the velocities of the two rods are the same and equal to v, this common velocity is equal to the center-of-mass velocity, therefore v=v_0/2+g sinθ t_0=g sinθ t_0+mgR sinθ/(B^2L^2). Subtracting the two equations gives du/dt=-(B^2L^2/(mR))u. Let λ=B^2L^2/(mR), then u decays exponentially. The relative displacement Δx=∫_0^{t_0}u dt. According to the problem statement, at t_0 the relative velocity decreases to zero, that is u(t_0)=0; from du/dt=-λu, Δx=(u(0)-u(t_0))/λ=v_0/λ can be obtained. Substituting v_0=2mgR sinθ/(B^2L^2) and λ=B^2L^2/(mR), obtains Δx=2m^2R^2g sinθ/(B^4L^4).
